# Ten years of outbreaks

## Two and a half centuries of models, then ten years of outbreaks

![](../figures/keynote-timeline.png){width="92%" fig-align="center"
fig-alt="A timeline. A compressed left segment carries small grey ticks
for Bernoulli 1760, Ross 1911, Kermack and McKendrick 1927, foot and
mouth 2001 and H1N1 2009. An expanded right segment carries four large
dots: Ebola in West Africa 2014 in grey, labelled watching; COVID-19
2020, mpox 2022 and Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the DRC
2026 in teal, labelled doing it, nowcasting and live."}

::: {.attribution}
Bernoulli 1760 after Dietz and Heesterbeek 2002,
[doi:10.1016/S0025-5564(02)00122-0](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0025-5564(02)00122-0)

· Kermack and McKendrick 1927,

· foot and mouth 2001, Ferguson, Donnelly and Anderson,
[doi:10.1126/science.1061020](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1061020)

[doi:10.1126/science.1176062](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1176062)

## 2014. Watching

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- CDC projected 1.4 million cases in Liberia and Sierra Leone by
  20 January 2015 without further intervention
- About 21,000 had occurred by mid January
- Camacho, Funk and colleagues estimated $R$, the number of new
  infections per infected person, by district in Sierra Leone
- Real-time modelling had arrived. Its overreach was public
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-funk2019-forecasts-panel.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Weekly Ebola incidence in Western Area, Sierra Leone, from
September 2014 to February 2015 as a thick black line, with one-week-ahead
forecasts as dots joined by a thin line and grey credible bands, peaking
near 350 cases a week in December 2014."}

::: {.attribution}
Meltzer et al., MMWR, September 2014,
[cdc.gov/mmwr su6303a1](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/su6303a1.htm)
· CDC's account of the 21,000, MMWR 2016,
[su6503a12](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/65/su/su6503a12.htm)
· Camacho et al., PLOS Currents Outbreaks, 10 February 2015
· Figure: panel B of Fig 2, Funk et al. 2019, PLOS Comput Biol,
[doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006785](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1006785),
CC-BY 4.0, downloaded 11 September 2026 and cropped
:::
:::
::::

## 2020. Doing it

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- $R_t$, the reproduction number over time, daily for several
  thousand locations
- A public dashboard from spring 2020 to March 2022
- Weekly estimates and forecasts to SPI-M-O, the UK government's
  modelling advisers
- "At least 80% but on time"
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-example-rt-panel.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Four panels of estimated reproduction number over time for
Australia, France, Germany and South Korea, each a green ribbon around
a dashed line at one, with an orange widening ribbon for the most recent
days where the estimate is still uncertain."}

::: {.attribution}
Abbott et al. 2020, Wellcome Open Research,
[doi:10.12688/wellcomeopenres.16006.1](https://doi.org/10.12688/wellcomeopenres.16006.1)
· [epiforecasts.io/covid](https://epiforecasts.io/covid/), repository
created 21 March 2020, last global estimates 31 March 2022
· figure and "several thousand locations" from the 25 March 2022 post
at [samabbott.co.uk][rt-post], copied from
`seabbs.github.io/_posts/2022-03-25-rt-reflections/example-rt.png` and
cropped to four of six panels, `scripts/keynote-crop.py`
· SPI-M-O: grant text, `composable-grant/coapplicant_details/sam.qmd`,
and the consensus statements on
[GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/spi-m-o-consensus-statement-on-covid-19-6-january-2021)
· "at least 80% but on time" from the 4 January 2023 post at
[samabbott.co.uk][iisa-post]
:::

## What came out of it

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Nowcasting, estimating what has already happened but has not yet
  been reported
- `EpiNow2` for $R_t$, `epinowcast` for nowcasting, `scoringutils` for
  evaluation, and the forecast hubs
- CDC used `EpiNow2` for its COVID-19 $R_t$ estimates to June 2026
- "In many cases the package is too complex for anyone else to use"
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-packages.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="A horizontal timeline from 2020 to 2026 with lollipops for
scoringutils, EpiNow and the Rt dashboard, EpiNow2, the European
COVID-19 Forecast Hub, epinowcast, epidist, EpiAware.jl,
primarycensored, baselinenowcast and BVDOutbreakSize, each at its first
commit or repository creation month."}

::: {.attribution}
First commits from the local clones, repository creation dates from the
GitHub API, 11 September 2026
· CDC, *Behind the Model: Nowcasting*, updated 30 January 2026,
[cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/cfa-behind-the-model/php/data-research/nowcasting.html)
· MMWR 73(46), 21 November 2024,
[cdc.gov/mmwr mm7346a3](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/wr/mm7346a3.htm)
· the CDC $R_t$ estimates page no longer names EpiNow2, read
11 September 2026; a search snippet reports a change of method for
dates after 1 June 2026,
[cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/cfa-modeling-and-forecasting/rt-estimates/index.html)
· quote from the JuliaCon 2026 roadmap deck,

· diagram this talk, `scripts/keynote-timeline.py`

## 2022. mpox

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Cases by symptom onset arrive late. The most recent days look like
  a fall
- Nowcasting for UKHSA, the UK Health Security Agency, with Overton and
  colleagues
- Ward et al. estimated the incubation period and serial interval from
  UK contact tracing. We wrote the editorial that ran beside it
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-overton2023-historical.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Two panels of daily mpox cases in England by symptom onset. Red
dots are the counts known on the nowcast date, blue dots the counts
eventually reported, a dashed black line the nowcast median and a grey
band its interval. The red dots fall to zero in the most recent days
while the nowcast and the later data do not."}

::: {.attribution}
Figure: Fig 7 of Overton, Abbott et al. 2023, *Nowcasting the 2022 mpox
outbreak in England*, PLOS Comput Biol,
[doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011463](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011463),
CC-BY 4.0, downloaded 11 September 2026
· Ward et al. 2022, BMJ,
[doi:10.1136/bmj-2022-073153](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2022-073153)
· Freeman, Abbott and Kurpiel 2022, BMJ editorial,
[doi:10.1136/bmj.o2504](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.o2504)
:::
:::
::::

## 2026. Live

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus, DRC. Declared 15 May
- A WHO emergency, a PHEIC, on 17 May
- 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths by 7 September
- Most infections are never confirmed. A joint model estimates the
  total
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/keynote-bvd-infections-sep-panel.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Left, modelled cumulative infections over time from February to
September 2026 as widening blue credible bands reaching about twelve
thousand. Right, the posterior density of cumulative infections at the
6 September cut-off, peaking near twelve thousand with a long right
tail."}

::: {.attribution}
[WHO DON617][don617], 10 September 2026, data to 7 September
· dates from [WHO DON602][don602]
· figure from [BVDOutbreakSize][bvd] release `results-1699`,
9 September 2026, data to SitRep 115 of 6 September, top row of the
joint model estimates on its analysis page, `scripts/keynote-crop.py`
:::
